extracted.intended_audience: students in a first advanced undergraduate mathematics / transition-to-proof course (learning how to write and read proofs about sets)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standard techniques for writing and checking proofs about sets: proving element membership, subset relations, set equality, Cartesian product identities, and example applications in number theory (e.g., perfect numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show a ∈ {x : P(x)}
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that a belongs to a set expressed in set-builder form {x : P(x)}, show that the property P(a) is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the set is {x ∈ S : P(x)}, first verify a ∈ S, then show P(a). (Examples: show 21 ∈ {x : x ∈ N and 7|x} by verifying 21 ∈ N and 7|21.)

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show a ∈ {x ∈ S : P(x)}
rubrics_metrics.description: When the set explicitly restricts to a universe S, membership requires both universe membership and the property: show a ∈ S and P(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-step verification: (1) Verify a ∈ S. (2) Show P(a) is true. The text emphasizes understanding rather than rote memorization, and gives examples with integers and power-set elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Prove A ⊆ B (Direct approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the conditional 'If a ∈ A then a ∈ B' by assuming a ∈ A and deducing a ∈ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: assume an arbitrary a ∈ A, use definitions and algebraic/logical manipulation to derive a ∈ B, conclude A ⊆ B. The direct approach usually yields the most straightforward proof; many examples follow this pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Prove A ⊆ B (Contrapositive approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish A ⊆ B by proving the contrapositive: assume a ∉ B and deduce a ∉ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the contrapositive is more expedient. The same logical structure applies: show 'if a ∉ B then a ∉ A' for arbitrary a, then conclude A ⊆ B.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Prove A ⊆ B (Proof by contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove A ⊆ B by assuming (a ∈ A) ∧ (a ∉ B) and deriving a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes this as an option alongside direct and contrapositive methods; use when assuming both leads quickly to an impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Prove A = B
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two sets are equal, prove both inclusions A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard two-step procedure: show A ⊆ B by an element argument, then show B ⊆ A similarly; conclude A = B. Several examples illustrate this (e.g., {n ∈ Z : 35|n} = {n : 5|n} ∩ {n : 7|n}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving subset/equality by element-chasing (general method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with an arbitrary element meeting the left-hand condition, use the definitions of the set operations involved, and deduce the required right-hand membership or property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the underlying method in most examples: assume x satisfies the left-hand set description, unpack definitions (divisibility, Cartesian product, intersection/union, power set), perform algebraic/logical deductions, then repackage as right-hand membership. Many worked examples (divisibility sets, Cartesian products) follow this pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using singletons and power sets to translate membership statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To deduce A ⊆ B from P(A) ⊆ P(B), use the fact that {a} ∈ P(A) for any a ∈ A, hence {a} ∈ P(B), hence a ∈ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 8.9: assume P(A) ⊆ P(B). For arbitrary a ∈ A, {a} ∈ P(A) so {a} ∈ P(B), therefore a ∈ B. This technique is useful when power sets are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set-equality/containment for Cartesian products
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove identities like A×(B∩C) = (A×B) ∩ (A×C), show both inclusions using the definition of Cartesian product: (x,y) ∈ A×B iff x ∈ A and y ∈ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical steps: assume (a,b) ∈ A×(B∩C), deduce a ∈ A and b ∈ B∩C, hence b ∈ B and b ∈ C, so (a,b) ∈ A×B and (a,b) ∈ A×C, hence in the intersection. Reverse inclusion is similar. The text gives both element-wise and algebraic/logical-manipulation proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case analysis for union or 'or' membership
rubrics_metrics.description: When membership is of the form X ∈ P(A) ∪ P(B), proceed by cases: either X ∈ P(A) or X ∈ P(B), and handle each case to reach the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving P(A) ∪ P(B) ⊆ P(A ∪ B): from X ∈ P(A) ∪ P(B) consider the two cases separately and show X ⊆ A ∪ B in each case. The text explicitly recommends case-splitting when the union leads naturally to two alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set equalities using logical/algebraic manipulation of set-builder predicates
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulate the logical formula inside set-builder notation using logical equivalences (e.g., P ↔ P ∧ P) and rearrangement to show two set-defining predicates are equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 8.13: rewrite Ax(B∩C) as {(x,y) : (x ∈ A) ∧ (y ∈ B ∧ y ∈ C)} then rearrange to show it equals (A×B) ∩ (A×C). The text warns this approach can be concise but sometimes difficult to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions of arithmetic relations (like divisibility) in set proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When sets are defined by arithmetic properties (e.g., {x ∈ Z : 18|x}), apply the definition (existence of integer c with x = 18c) to deduce other divisibility facts (e.g., 6|x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show {x ∈ Z : 18|x} ⊆ {x ∈ Z : 6|x} by writing x = 18c = 6(3c). Use prime factorization when proving converses (e.g., intersection of 5|n and 7|n implies 35|n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining proof techniques inside a proof (nested arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof may contain other proofs inside it (e.g., an existence proof may include a proof by contradiction to show an auxiliary fact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text examples: constructive existence proofs interleaved with a contradiction argument to show log2 9 is irrational; chapters encourage being alert to combinations of techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using known algebraic/analytic formulas (e.g., geometric series) as a tool in set membership proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring in relevant formulas (such as sum of geometric series) to compute sums or other quantities required to establish set membership in number-theoretic contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving numbers of the form 2^{n-1}(2^n−1) are perfect uses the geometric series identity sum_{k=0}^{n-1} 2^k = 2^n−1 to show the sum of proper divisors equals the number. The text explicitly invokes Equation (8.1) in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using prime factorization arguments for divisibility/equality proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving statements about divisibility or product-based set membership, use prime factorization to argue which primes must appear and conclude divisibility properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show {n : 5|n} ∩ {n : 7|n} ⊆ {n : 35|n}, note that if 5|a and 7|a then both prime factors 5 and 7 appear in a's prime factorization, hence 35|a.
